title: Spring Into Solid Sleep Habits
body:
With spring around the corner, we are close to setting our clocks an hour ahead on March 8. This is the perfect time to dial in good sleep habits to improve focus and performance.

Poor sleep is the culprit behind many issues for youth athletes such as:

  • Incomplete recovery between activity

  • Decreased growth hormone release

  • Increased risk of injury

  • Poor decision-making/brain function in games and school

  • Mood swings and poor emotional regulation

  • Decreased immune system function

  • Reduced strength and power output

Needless to say the best legal performance enhancer is sleep and yet many athletes are falling well short of what is needed to be at their best.

Youth athletes should be targeting 8-10 hours of sleep per night (sometimes even more).

Here’s what else matters for good sleep:

  • Aiming for consistent wake up/go to bed times - out body likes predictability and will respond well to a routine

  • Screens off an hour before bed

  • A cool (approximately 68 degrees), dark room

  • Establish a wind down routine (stretch, read, journal, etc.)

  • Avoiding caffeine after 3pm

  • Morning sunlight exposure upon waking

Given that this is a lot steps, I encourage youth athletes to adopt 1-2 of these habits, discover what works best for them and stick to that. Very few athletes are doing any of these so small steps in the right direction will give you a leg up on the competition.

Don’t be overwhelmed by this information. Start basic and build out! If you are already sleeping 8-10 hours, you are on the right track.

title: The Biggest Mistake I'm Seeing Athletes Make
body:
This February, as we transition from winter to spring sports, athletes must focus on planning out their approach to this transition.

For athletes approaching the end of their season, it is a MUST they take time to rest before they move onto their next sport or club sports. I am seeing overuse injuries in athletes across multiple sports and that will only continue to increase if they don’t significantly reduce practice and playing time for 2-4 weeks after their season ends.

Taking time off can feel counterproductive, but it is critical to allow joints, muscles and the mind to recover from the stresses of the season. Over time, strategic periods of rest will help offset, injury and burnout while helping support long-term performance success.

For athletes entering their seasons, most teams open the year with a huge spike in workload over practice, fitness and team lifting sessions. Most kids have not done enough to prepare for the demands of the first few weeks of their sport.

Without fail, this drives inflammation/soreness, tendon pain and loss of mobility. All of this can increase injury risk and leave the athlete in a compromised position entering the regular season.

While some of this is unavoidable, athletes and their parents need to do the following:

  1. Advocate for coaches to have a more structured increase in workload in the preaseason - sport coaches need to be held responsible for intelligent, safe practice plans

  2. Dial in their sleep, nutrition and daily mobility/prep work

  3. Prepare with a knowledgeable performance coach so they can either handle the increased workload or have a resource to help them navigate any injuries that occur with the workload spike.

Ultimately, these transitions between seasons, are where athletes often go wrong and can severely set back their progression/career. The goal should be to maximize performance over a four-year period rather than burn the candle at both ends month after month and flame out before the end of high school.

title: Returning Properly From a Concussion
body:
A concussion is a brain injury that many athletes suffer while playing their sport. They are sustained by a blow to the head, being struck in the head by an object or by a fall in which the head strikes the ground.

Concussions vary in severity, but symptoms include:

  • Headaches

  • Dizziness

  • Nausea/vomiting

  • Sensitivity to light and noise

  • Balance problems

  • Issues with concentration/memory

  • Irritability/mood swings

  • Irregular sleep habits

After suffering any head injury, athletes should be aware of these symptoms and report them to a coach or medical professional such as an Athletic Trainer, Physical Therapist or Doctor.

In my experience, many athletes fail to report symptoms or do not have the resources available to assist them in the aftermath of a concussion.

If this is the case, athletes must take some initiative to protect themselves as suffering multiple concussions in close proximity to each other can be very bad for the brain.

In this instance, here is a guide for athletes to protect themselves and return to sport safely. That being said, make it a priority to use caution and consult a healthcare provider to assist in your return to sport.

  • The athlete must be symptom-free before starting physical activity.

    • To progress, limit screen time and and tasks that require intense focus

    • Skipping school and social activities is a wise choice

    • This period can last up to several days - be patient!

  • Stage 1: Light aerobic activity

    • Aim for 15-20 min walking on a treadmill or a casual exercise bike ride

    • Do not progress past this stage until it is completed without symptoms

  • Stage 2: Resistance training

    • A low intensity lower body lift can be attempted after passing stage one

    • If symptom free, a low intensity upper body lift can be attempted the next day

    • If symptom free, intensity can be increased with resistance training

  • Stage 3: Sport-specific drills in the gym

    • Sprinting, cutting, and jumping can be performed in a controlled gym setting

  • Stage 4: Non-contact practice

  • Stage 5: Full contact practice

    • Get medical clearance for this

  • Stage 6: Return to competition

Notes:

  • Do not skip stages

  • Do not advance more than one stage per day

  • If you experience symptoms, regress to the previous stage and re-pass it

  • If you return to play with symptoms, suffering another concussion can lead to more intense symptoms and can be extremely dangerous especially to younger athletes.

  • Be patient and heed your symptoms. Seek medical help if you suffer a concussion and have a plan to return gradually.

title: Road Warriors: Peak Performance for Away Games
body:
We’re in the thick of club soccer season and that means:

  • Long road trips both flying and driving

  • Weekends with multiple games

  • And plenty of opportunities for poor sleep, nutrition and hydration


While road trips are challenging to performance, players who can maintain as much of their normal routine as possible tend to fare better.

Here’s what to focus on:

💧Drink water consistently throughout the trip and include electrolyte drinks especially before and during games.

🍝 Focus on carbs up to 24 hours before games. After games mix your carbs with protein for recovery.

😴 Sleep can be tricky with travel, but getting as close as you can to 8 hours per night will be a game-changer

🏃🏻Sitting in a car for hours means getting out during breaks to walk around and stretch. Doing a mobility routine in your hotel room before bed helps too.

While ticking all these boxes is sometimes impossible on the road, make an effort to complete at least some of them. It will make a huge difference!

title: Compression vs. Ice: Which Is Better?
body:
Currently, I have several athletes in the middle of their respective seasons dealing with the bumps and bruises that come with competition.

Swelling, tendon/joint pain and bone bruises are quite common for knees, hips, ankles and shoulders.

Often we see most athletes treat these ailments with ice to relieve pain and reduce swelling.

While there is a time and a place for ice, I urge most of the my athletes to rely more on compression as their primary recovery modality and here’s why:

  • Compression promotes extra blood flow to affected areas.

  • Increased blood flow moves out waste product and reduces fluid buildup/stiffness.

  • Compression provides extra stability for joints.

  • Compression generally offers a high level of pain relief.

  • Compression helps eliminate excessive inflammation around an affected area.

Meanwhile, ice actually slows down blood flow, which can affect the removal of waste product and promote fluid buildup. And in some cases it can be too effective at reducing swelling.

It is important to remember that an inflammatory response is something we want in order to promote healing. Obviously we want to manage excessive inflammation but we do not want to eliminate it entirely.

Thus, for long-term healing and proper management of swelling/inflammation, compression is far superior to ice.

However, if there is a quick turnaround between competitions and an athlete gets significant pain relief from ice, it can be a viable option.

Be mindful of this when determining your options for recovery. Typically compression is better.

title: A Simple Nutrition Checklist for Athletes
body:
Recently I have been taking a deeper dive into each of my athletes’ nutrition habits. The same basic problems seem to be common for most:

  • Missing meals especially breakfast

  • Not eating enough protein

  • Underfueling before and after games/practice/workouts

  • Not drinking enough water

So I compiled a simple checklist for several athletes to track their daily nutrition habits.

If athletes are not checking these boxes, they are leaving tremendous gains on the table. Once these pillars of nutrition become habitual, there can be a deeper discussion about supplements and caloric intake.

title: The Buzz Around Caffeine
body:
Caffeine is one of the most widely used performance-enhancing substances in the athletic world—and for good reason.

It is a stimulant that:

  • Improves focus and reaction time

  • Increases endurance

  • Delays onset of fatigue

The best time for athletes to use caffeine is about 30-60 minutes before training or competition. Dosage can vary based on how big you are and your caffeine tolerance. Consuming too much caffeine can lead to jitters, impaired sleep and increased heart rate - all of which some athletes find disruptive to performance.

Start with 80mg or so and find the amount that works best for you. Keep in mind the NCAA limits caffeine consumption to 500mg in competitions.

It important to remember that caffeine is not a replacement for the fundamentals: sleep and proper nutrition. Dial those in first and then worry about supplementation. Then caffeine can be even more effective.

title: Lift In-Season, Stay Strong
body:
With most high school athletes participating in their sport(s) year round, strength training is a key element that often gets lost in the shuffle.

While I would never discourage a basketball player from playing, year-round strength training is essential to keep athletes resilient and developing physically.

And it doesn’t have to be complicated. A simple, well-structured program should get the job done.

Here’s what Santa Barbara High School varsity soccer athletes are doing in-season:

DB Stepup 3x5 each way
Vertical Jump 3x5
Physio Hamstring Curl 3x10
Inverted Row or Pull-Up 3x10 or 3x6
Push-Up to Downward Dog 3x10

5 exercises. 20 minutes. That’s it. Try to add weight session over session, but keep the total number of working sets low to avoid unnecessary fatigue.

Keep it simple. Stay strong.

title: Don't Forget About Fats
body:
With all the focus on carbs and protein, fats often get overlooked as a macronutrient, but they’re crucial for performance and recovery.

Here’s why:

Long-Lasting Energy – Fats fuel endurance and longer activities when carbs run low.
Nutrient Absorption – They help absorb key vitamins (A, D, E, K) needed for growth and recovery.
Hormone Production – Fats support hormone balance, including those that build and repair muscles.

Examples of healthy fats:
🥑 Avocados
🫒 Olive oil
🐟 Fatty fish (salmon, tuna)
🥜 Nuts, seeds, nut butter

Don’t skip fats—they help you perform, recover, and stay strong!

title: What to Make of the 2025 NCAA Recruiting Changes
body:
We are likely to see some big changes to the recruiting landscape in 2025 NCAA sports such as:

  • Elimination of scholarship limits - each NCAA sport will have expanded scholarship opportunities for each rostered athlete

  • Institution of roster limits - each NCAA sport will have a cap on how many players they can roster

  • Colleges will establish a Names, Image and Likeness (NIL) budget to pay student athletes

As this will certainly make recruiting more competitive, Jack was able to talk with Senior Recruiting Analyst, Michael Babich from SportsRecruits.com to make sense of all the changes.

This 20-minute podcast covers the pros and cons of these changes for both male and female athletes. Michael also provides some advice on how high school athletes can enhance their recruiting profiles and draw interest from college programs.

In addition to the podcast, Michael has also written this article for those interested in learning more.

Thanks to Michael for coming on, and for those athletes interested in getting further help with the recruiting process check out SportsRecruits.

title: Carbohydrates Are the Secret Stuff
body:
A few weeks ago we highlighted the first of three macronutrients by discussing the importance of protein. However, Carbohydrates are equally important for athletes and here’s why:

  • They are the primary energy source for the body - Carbohydrates need to be consumed at every meal and especially before and after practice, training and games.

  • They are protein sparing - When protein is utilized as an energy source, it is then unable to fulfill its primary job of repairing and building muscle tissues. Carbohydrate consumption allows protein to play its proper role.

  • They help brain function - Carbs help maintain focus, decision-making and memory.

When carbs are broken down in our bodies, a simple sugar called glucose is formed and is used as energy to complete actions as complex as dunking a basketball or as simple as blinking your eyes.

It is painfully obvious when an athlete is not getting enough carbs. They usually feel flat, lack explosiveness and endurance and tend to underperform in training and games.

Ensure you are eating carbs at every meal and before activity to get the most out of your body. Examples of carbs include breads, fruits, yogurt, pasta, oatmeal, beans, and certain vegetables such as potatoes, corn, carrots and peas.

title: Don't Skip Breakfast
body:
The vast majority of high school athletes we work with skip breakfast at least several times per week. This is incredibly damaging to performance and can blunt the positive effects of quality training.

Skipping breakfast results in the following:

  • Decreased energy, productivity and decision-making ability

  • Poorer diet quality and decreased muscle mass

  • Decreased mental health and a lowered immune system

So many athletes work hard. They practice upwards of three hours per day, play in multiple games each weekend, train in the weight room and also balance a hectic school schedule.

If nutrition isn’t part of the equation, many athletes simply fall behind their peers because they quite literally run out of gas.

Don’t let all that work go to waste because food wasn’t a priority. Skipping breakfast puts every athlete at a major disadvantage.

Here are a few strategies to try and start making breakfast part of your day:

  • Find foods you like (Some of Jack’s favorites are smoothies, overnight oats, eggs, yogurt, waffles, steak and hash browns)

  • Make it the night before

  • Meal prep all your breakfasts over the weekend

  • Ask your parents to help you plan out and prepare breakfasts

  • Wake up earlier to prepare/eat it

  • If you aren’t hungry when you wake up, pack a breakfast for the ride to school

  • Be disciplined

While food quality is important, start by ensuring you get breakfast everyday preferably with 30-50 grams of protein.

title: The Three Pillars of Sleep
body:
A good night’s sleep might be one the biggest keys to maintaining a high level of performance and lowering risk of injury.

This short podcast by Dr. Erik Korem outlines the three crucial pillars needed to maximize proper sleep:

  • Duration - 7-9 hours per night

  • Onset - Going to bed before midnight

  • Consistency - Keeping your sleep schedule the same every night

Obviously, life doesn’t always allow us to maintain these habits every night. Adhere to these pillars as best you can and don’t give up if it takes a while to dial them into your life. As with everything, there are ups and downs. But quality sleep is worth prioritizing for any serious athlete.

title: Should Athletes Take Creatine?
body:
Creatine is one of the most studied supplements on the planet and has numerous benefits for athletic performance including:

  • Improved strength and power

  • Faster recovery

  • Increased explosiveness

  • Possible cognitive benefits

With such a wide range of positive adaptations, all high school athletes should consider using creatine, provided they have no kidney-related illnesses or issues.

Ensure that any supplements taken are NSF certified and only purchase creatine monohydrate with no additional ingredients. Here is a list of some of the best creatine products on the market:

  • Thorne

  • Klean

  • Momentous (Jack uses this brand)

  • Core (Gummies instead of powder)

Athletes should take 5g of creatine monohydrate daily. Some brands encourage a loading phase, but this is unnecessary.

Remember that supplements are a useful tool, but not a substitute for a proper nutrition and sleep.

title: How to Win the College Recruiting Process
body:
Becoming a college athlete can be a challenging, stressful process. Obviously, performance in your sport and a solid academic record are essential pieces in getting offers and attention from coaches.

However, college coaches are often bombarded with responsibilities and may not prioritize you even after expressing interest.

In cases like this, it’s important to understand the recruiting landscape and how to be proactive in selling yourself as both an athlete and human being.

This latest podcast from Jack details how to stand out from the pack when interacting with college coaches. Character, work ethic and personality are all huge factors in helping coaches extend offers to high school athletes. These are all very controllable and matter to some coaches almost as much as academic and athletic performance.

Additionally, check out the the NCSA Recruiting Information website to familiarize yourself with the recruiting schedule for each sport. Timing is everything when reaching out to schools. Communicate with coaches whenever possible to show your interest and practice marketing yourself!

title: NCAA Eligibility Requirements
body:
Jack recently did a podcast outlining the academic requirements for high school athletes planning to play in NCAA or NAIA sports in college. You can listen to it right here.

In addition, here are a few links that provide more information directly from the NCAA.

  • NCAA Eligibility Center

  • Find your high school’s core courses approved by the NCAA

  • DI Academic Requirements

  • DII Academic Requirements

  • More about amateurism status

Athletes, it is critical to speak with your school counsellor and ensure you understand the timeline of events for each year of high school. Do not fall behind and see that all obligations are met on time. The recruiting process is challenging enough and this will make it easier on yourself, college coaches and admissions departments.
